The core trade-offs # The analog-to-digital converter (ADC) is the bridge between the analog and digital worlds. When selecting one, it is easy to fall into the trap of looking only at bit depth and sampling rate. In reality, ADC performance is determined by a set of mutually constrained parameters; understanding the physical nature of each parameter and the trade-offs between them is the real foundation of correct selection.
Three core contradictions dominate:
Contradiction Nature Speed vs. accuracy Higher sampling rates leave less settling time per sample, so quantization and thermal noise dominate and the effective resolution drops. High-speed ADCs typically deliver only 8–12 effective bits; high-precision ADCs usually sample at only kSPS rates. Channel count vs. synchronization Sharing one ADC across channels (multiplexing) is cheap and supports many channels, but channels sample at slightly different times. A dedicated ADC per channel (simultaneous sampling) is expensive and large, but time-aligned. Bandwidth vs. noise Wider analog bandwidth lets high-frequency signals through, but also admits more thermal noise. A low-bandwidth ADC acts as a natural anti-aliasing filter with less noise, at the cost of attenuating high frequencies. Analog bandwidth # Analog bandwidth is the highest frequency range that the ADC’s front-end analog circuits can pass without distortion. It is determined jointly by the input buffer, the sample-and-hold circuit, and the internal front-end frequency response.
The industry standard metric is the -3 dB bandwidth: the frequency at which the output amplitude of a sine wave drops to 70.7% of its low-frequency reference value (half the power, i.e. -3 dB):
$$f_{-3\text{dB}}: \text{output amplitude} = 0.707 \times \text{low-frequency amplitude}$$The -3 dB point is not where the signal disappears; it is where attenuation becomes noticeable. Beyond it, the signal keeps decaying until it is buried in noise.
Bandwidth is mainly determined by: the gain-bandwidth product (GBW) of the input amplifier, the charge/discharge speed of the sample-and-hold capacitor, the RC time constants of the internal divider network and switches, and the parasitic parameters of the package and PCB traces.
When the input frequency exceeds the analog bandwidth: high-frequency components are attenuated (measured amplitude reads low), phase lags differently per frequency component (waveform distortion), square waves become rounded at the edges, and the signal-to-noise ratio degrades.
A key point: a high sampling rate does not mean high bandwidth. Many ADCs are rated at 200 kSPS yet have only a few kHz of analog bandwidth — sampling fast is not the same as resolving fast signals.
Selection principle: analog bandwidth should be 1.5–2× the highest signal frequency. Not exactly equal, because at the -3 dB point the signal is already attenuated by 30%; the margin keeps the in-band response flat and amplitude error small.
Sampling rate # Sampling rate is the number of complete conversions per second (SPS). It sets the time resolution of the digital representation.
Nyquist sampling theorem. To reconstruct a band-limited signal without distortion, the sampling rate must be strictly greater than twice the highest signal frequency:
$$f_s > 2 f_{max}$$If this is violated, aliasing occurs: components above the Nyquist frequency fold back into the low-frequency band and mix with real signals, and cannot be separated afterwards. The alias frequency is:
$$f_{alias} = |f_{signal} - \text{round}(f_{signal}/f_s) \times f_s|$$In practice, engineering rarely uses the Nyquist minimum; three tiers are common:
Sampling choice Multiple of $f_{max}$ Use case Characteristics Nyquist minimum $2\times$ Static / quasi-static measurement Anti-aliasing filter mandatory; waveform easily distorted Typical $5\text{–}10\times$ General data acquisition Good waveform reconstruction, moderate storage High-fidelity $10\text{–}20\times$ Vibration analysis, instruments High fidelity, large storage Oscilloscope-grade $>20\times$ High-speed transient capture Sharp edge details, high cost A higher sampling rate is not always better. Storage grows linearly (10× the rate is 10× the data), power consumption rises roughly proportionally, downstream filtering and FFT load increases, and the effective number of bits (ENOB) drops because settling time is insufficient. The principle: the lowest sampling rate that meets the requirement is the optimal one.
Multi-channel architectures and synchronization # Feature Time-multiplexed (MUX) Simultaneous Architecture One ADC + analog switch Independent S/H + ADC per channel Cost Low (shared ADC) High (per-channel hardware) Channel count Many (8–16 typical) Few (2–8) Sampling instant Channels offset in sequence All channels at the same instant Inter-channel skew ~1 sampling period Nanoseconds Typical use Temperature, slow monitoring TDOA positioning, vibration analysis When is simultaneous sampling mandatory? Any application that measures time differences: TDOA localization, phase-difference interferometry, multi-channel vibration modal analysis, power quality (multi-phase current/voltage phase), and sonar array processing. The reason is straightforward: to measure the time difference between two signals, both must be sampled at the same instant. If the ADC itself has inter-channel timing errors, those errors contaminate the measured time difference and cannot be removed in software.
Can multiplexing be compensated in software? Partially. Fixed inter-channel offsets can be calibrated once and corrected. But dynamic offsets that vary with temperature and signal amplitude, plus random deviations from sampling-clock jitter, cannot.
Channel skew # Channel skew is the tiny difference between the actual sampling instants of different channels, even on a simultaneous-sampling ADC. It is usually specified in ps or ns.
Skew mainly comes from: differences in sample-and-hold switch turn-on time, propagation-delay differences in the analog front-end buffers, trace-length differences on the PCB, and device-parameter mismatch from process variation.
Skew translates directly into distance error in positioning:
$$\Delta d = v_{sound} \times \Delta t$$With a sound speed of about 1500 m/s in water:
Inter-channel skew Distance error Application grade 1 ns 1.5 μm High-precision USBL 10 ns 15 μm General industrial measurement 100 ns 150 μm Standard positioning 1 μs 1.5 mm Consumer products 10 μs 15 mm Coarse positioning Selection principle: channel skew must be much smaller than the smallest time difference the system must measure. For example, to measure a 1 μs time difference, the skew should be below 100 ns to keep 1% accuracy.
Phase matching # Phase matching is the phase difference between channel outputs when identical, same-phase sine waves drive different ADC channels. It is the frequency-domain manifestation of channel skew:
$$\Delta\phi = 2\pi f \times \Delta t$$The same skew produces a larger phase error at higher frequencies: at low frequencies it is negligible, at high frequencies it is amplified.
Why it matters. Interferometric positioning (e.g. USBL phase-difference direction finding) works by comparing the phase difference of the same signal received at two transducers to compute the angle of arrival. The ADC’s own channel phase difference adds directly to the measurement:
$$\epsilon_\theta \approx \frac{\Delta\phi}{d/\lambda}$$where $d$ is transducer spacing and $\lambda$ the wavelength.
Phase matching is not a fixed value; it varies with frequency. In the low band (DC to ~1/10 of bandwidth) it is near zero; in the mid band (1/10 to 1/2) it grows roughly linearly; near or beyond the bandwidth it deteriorates rapidly while amplitude also drops. When the signal frequency approaches the ADC’s bandwidth limit, phase consistency degrades sharply — both amplitude and phase become unreliable.
Clock jitter # Clock jitter is the short-term deviation of the actual sampling instant from the ideal one. Even a perfect oscillator has small random fluctuations.
Jitter injects amplitude error proportional to signal frequency:
$$V_{error} = 2\pi f_{signal} \times t_{jitter} \times V_{amplitude}$$The same jitter is harmless at 1 kHz but can be fatal at 100 MHz — which is why high-speed, high-precision ADCs demand a very clean clock source.
Converted to a signal-to-noise penalty:
$$\text{SNR}_{jitter} \approx -20\log_{10}(2\pi f t_{jitter})$$ Signal frequency SNR loss, 1 ns jitter SNR loss, 10 ps jitter 1 kHz -14 dB -34 dB 10 kHz -10 dB -30 dB 100 kHz -6 dB -26 dB 1 MHz -2 dB -22 dB 10 MHz negligible -18 dB Selection principle: the higher the signal frequency, the more sensitive the system is to jitter. High-speed acquisition systems must use a low-jitter clock source (crystal oscillator or dedicated clock chip), never an ordinary RC oscillator.
Input noise and effective resolution # Nominal vs. effective resolution. The nominal bit depth is the theoretical quantization precision, but the smallest signal change actually resolvable is usually much smaller than the nominal value, because input noise exists:
$$\text{LSB} = V_{FS} / 2^N$$If the noise amplitude is 5 LSB, any signal change below 5 LSB is buried in noise and cannot be resolved.
ENOB (Effective Number of Bits) is the comprehensive figure of merit that folds noise, distortion, and jitter into an equivalent bit loss:
$$\text{ENOB} = (\text{SINAD} - 1.76) / 6.02$$Typical values: an ideal 16-bit ADC achieves ≈15.5 bits; a real 16-bit ADC ≈14–15 bits; a high-speed 12-bit ADC ≈10–11 bits; a cheap 8-bit ADC ≈7–7.5 bits.
Noise budget decomposition. Total system noise is layered: front-end noise (sensor + preamp thermal and bias-current noise, usually the largest), ADC thermal noise (thermal and flicker noise inside the chip), quantization noise (inherent, fixed), power-supply noise (ripple coupling into the analog input), and digital crosstalk (switching noise through parasitic coupling). The largest source is usually not the ADC itself but the front-end and the power supply — upgrading to a higher-bit ADC often yields little; reducing front-end noise first is the right path.
Oversampling. If the noise is predominantly white, oversampling improves effective resolution: each 4× oversampling gains 1 effective bit. Random white noise cancels under averaging while the signal accumulates, so the SNR improves. The cost is a 4× increase in data rate.
Selection principles by application # Application Priority Typical configuration Notes High-speed capture (oscilloscope/transient) Sampling rate > bandwidth > bits > channels 12-bit, >100 MSPS, >50 MHz BW Bits beyond 8–12 add little; speed and bandwidth matter High-precision DC/slow measurement Bits > input noise > linearity > sampling rate 24-bit, 1–100 kSPS, low-noise front end Sigma-delta ADC; precision over speed Multi-channel TDOA/phase positioning Sync architecture > skew > phase matching > rate > bandwidth 12–16-bit, simultaneous, skew <10 ns Simultaneous sampling is mandatory; never MUX Communication demodulation (FSK/PSK) Bandwidth > sampling rate > SNR > channels 12–16-bit, 2–5× signal bandwidth Bandwidth must cover the whole band Vibration/modal analysis Channels > sync > phase matching > bandwidth > rate 16–24-bit, simultaneous, wide band Inter-channel phase consistency drives modal accuracy How the parameters constrain each other # ADC parameters are not independent; understanding the coupling is what makes a reasonable trade-off possible.
Speed vs. accuracy. Higher sampling rates shorten settling time, degrading linearity, raising noise, and lowering ENOB. Rule of thumb: doubling the sampling rate costs roughly 0.5–1 bit of ENOB. Bandwidth vs. noise. White-noise power is proportional to bandwidth: $$V_{noise} \propto \sqrt{BW}$$Doubling the bandwidth adds 41% more noise, so wide-bandwidth ADCs need better front-end filtering.
Channels vs. cost vs. synchronization. More channels push toward multiplexing (cheap) at the cost of synchronization; simultaneous multi-channel sampling scales cost roughly per channel — each synchronized channel needs its own sample-and-hold and ADC. Sampling rate vs. data volume vs. processing. Raising the sampling rate raises not only the ADC cost but storage, transport, and processing cost across the whole data chain. There is no “best” parameter combination — only the combination best matched to the application. Identify the dominant requirement (speed, precision, synchronization, or channel count), choose the optimal ADC along that dimension, and let the others merely meet basic needs.
References # Analog Devices. MT-001: Taking the Mystery out of the Infamous Formula, “SNR = 6.02N + 1.76 dB”. (PDF) Analog Devices. MT-002: What the Nyquist Criterion Means to Your Sampled Data System Design. (PDF) Analog Devices. MT-101: Decimation and Interpolation. (PDF) Texas Instruments. A lesson in ENOB. (PDF) Texas Instruments. Understanding Data Converters. (link)

The basic principle # Sound travels at roughly 1500 m/s in seawater — far slower than electromagnetic waves (3 × 10⁸ m/s). This low speed is precisely what makes acoustic positioning feasible: if sound were as fast as light, a few milliseconds of time difference would correspond to tens of kilometers, and nothing could be measured. Because sound is slow, measuring time differences and converting them to distances becomes practical.
The core formula is simple:
$$d = v \times t$$where $d$ is the distance, $v$ the sound speed, and $t$ the propagation time. For example, a propagation time of 10 ms gives $d = 0.01 \times 1500 = 15$ m. Every underwater acoustic positioning method ultimately measures time or phase, converts it to distance, and determines position through multi-point intersection.
The geometry of localization. In two dimensions, knowing one distance places the target on a circle; two distances intersect at two points; three distances determine a unique position. In three dimensions, at least four distance measurements are required.
The effect of sound speed. The sound speed is not a constant — it varies with temperature, salinity, and depth, typically between 1450 and 1550 m/s. High-precision systems correct for this using a sound speed profile (SSP); low-precision ranging can simply use the 1500 m/s approximation.
Positioning methods # TOA (Time of Arrival) — ranging # TOA is the most basic ranging method: the transmitter sends a pulse at $t_1$, the receiver receives it at $t_2$, and the time difference $\Delta t = t_2 - t_1$ times the sound speed gives the distance:
$$d = v \times (t_2 - t_1)$$The principle is simple and accuracy depends on time measurement precision. The catch is clock synchronization: both ends must share a common time reference, otherwise the time difference is wrong. Two independent MCUs with a 1 ms clock error introduce a 1.5 m distance error. Real systems often use a transponder (reply) scheme: the receiver immediately sends back an acknowledgment pulse, and the transmitter measures the round-trip time, divides by two, and multiplies by the sound speed — sidestepping synchronization at the cost of both ends being able to transmit.
TDOA (Time Difference of Arrival) — hyperbolic positioning # TDOA does not require knowing the absolute transmission time; it only needs the time difference between the same signal arriving at different receivers. The time difference between two receivers maps to a distance difference, and the set of points with a constant distance difference forms a hyperbola:
$$\Delta d = v \times (t_2 - t_1)$$Two receivers → one hyperbola (the position lies on it); three receivers → two hyperbolas intersect → 2D localization; four receivers → 3D localization. This is the core principle of LBL (Long Baseline) systems. The key implementations are multi-channel synchronized sampling and cross-correlation to extract time differences. The difficulty is multi-channel time synchronization: timing accuracy must reach the microsecond level for millimeter-level ranging. The larger the hydrophone spacing, the larger the time difference and the smaller the relative error — which is why the method is called “long baseline”: longer baselines give higher accuracy.
AOA (Angle of Arrival) — beamforming # AOA measures the direction from which the signal arrives. Two or more hydrophones form an array; the signal reaches different hydrophones at slightly different times (phase differences), from which the incidence angle is derived:
$$\sin\theta = \frac{v \times \Delta t}{d}$$where $d$ is the hydrophone spacing and $\Delta t$ the time difference. Knowing both angle and distance locates the target. This is the principle of USBL (Ultra-Short Baseline) systems — the array spacing is very small and angles are measured via phase differences.
The difficulty is that angular errors are amplified by distance: a 1° angle error gives a 17 cm position error at 10 m, but 1.7 m at 100 m. USBL is therefore accurate at close range and degrades at long range.
Phase-difference ranging # Instead of measuring pulse arrival times, this method measures the phase difference of the carrier, which is proportional to distance:
$$\Delta\varphi = 2\pi \times \frac{d}{\lambda}$$where the wavelength $\lambda = v/f$. Accuracy is excellent (millimeter level). But phase is measured modulo $2\pi$, so the result is ambiguous — a measured 90° could mean 0.25 wavelengths or 1.25 wavelengths traveled. Practical systems combine TOA for coarse ranging and phase difference for fine ranging. The classic difficulty is the integer-cycle ambiguity: at 70 kHz the wavelength is about 2.1 cm, so every 2.1 cm the phase wraps once; ranging over meters requires knowing how many full wavelengths were crossed. GNSS positioning faces the same problem.
System classification: LBL / SBL / USBL # Acoustic positioning systems are classified by baseline length — the spacing between hydrophones:
Type Baseline Principle Accuracy Characteristics LBL (long) Hundreds to thousands of meters Seabed transponders, TDOA hyperbolic intersection Highest (meter level) Accurate but hard to deploy; requires transponders on the seabed SBL (short) A few to tens of meters Ship-mounted array, TDOA + AOA Medium Deployed on the ship; needs an underwater transponder USBL (ultra-short) Centimeters Compact array, phase-difference angle Medium (meter level) Small and easy to install; accuracy limited by angular error LBL: 3–4 transponders are deployed on the seabed to form a baseline array. The vehicle measures its distance to each transponder and intersects the range circles to locate itself. Highest accuracy, unaffected by water depth, but deployment and recovery are cumbersome — suited to long-term fixed sites.
SBL: The hydrophone array is mounted on the ship’s hull with meter-to-decameter spacing. With one underwater transponder, the ship measures range and bearing to compute relative position. More flexible than LBL, but accuracy is affected by ship attitude and water depth.
USBL: The array is compact (centimeter level), mounted on the ship’s hull or on an ROV. Angles are measured by phase difference, combined with ranging to obtain position. Small, easy to install, and the most common choice for consumer-grade and small ROVs. A single 70 kHz transmit-receive pair is the basic building block of USBL.
Technology roadmap # Year Event Significance 1963 USS Thresher sinking Triggered development; the origin of modern acoustic positioning, gave rise to SBL 1965 Alvin submersible with ALNAV acoustic navigation First practical underwater acoustic navigation system 1970 Cestone, Precise Underwater Navigation Systematized early underwater navigation principles 1972 Watkins & Schevill, TDOA hyperbolic method Established the mathematical foundation of TDOA 1972 Davies, near-bottom acoustic navigation comparison Analyzed LBL-class hyperbolic systems 1980s LBL commercialization Acoustic positioning moved from military to civil use 2000s USBL miniaturization, low-cost options Consumer ROVs and small platforms began to adopt it 2020s Sparse LBL, single-beacon, multi-sensor fusion Lower deployment cost, miniaturization Implementation essentials and difficulties # Method comparison # Method Core implementation Main difficulty Accuracy TOA ranging Pulse edge detection, high-precision timing Clock synchronization cm–dm level TDOA positioning Multi-channel synchronized sampling, cross-correlation Multi-channel sync, baseline geometry meter level AOA angle Small-spacing array, phase-difference angle Angular error grows with distance meter level (close range) Phase-difference ranging Continuous carrier, I/Q quadrature demodulation Integer-cycle ambiguity mm–cm level Three common challenges # 1. Non-uniform sound speed. Temperature, salinity, and depth all affect sound speed (1450–1550 m/s). The sound speed profile varies with depth and rays bend rather than travel straight. High-precision positioning requires ray-tracing corrections; low-precision ranging uses the 1500 m/s approximation.
2. Multipath. Sound reflects off the surface and seabed, so the receiver sees reflected paths alongside the direct path. Reflected and direct signals overlap, widening pulses and blurring edges, increasing timing errors. This is why shallow-water positioning is harder than deep-water — multipath is severe in shallow water.
3. The bandwidth–distance trade-off. High frequencies (e.g. 70 kHz) give good directionality and accuracy but attenuate quickly and cover short ranges; low frequencies (e.g. 10 kHz) travel far but have poor directionality and lower accuracy. Once the transducer frequency is chosen, range and accuracy are largely fixed.
Positioning architectures: USBL, piUSBL, LBL, DVL # Beyond the baseline classification, real platforms choose between four architectures, trading accuracy, cost, and deployment effort:
Architecture Principle Accuracy Cost Use case USBL (ship-mounted) Ship array measures slant range + bearing 0.1–1% of slant range $10k–100k Ship-towed ROV tracking piUSBL (on-board) Robot array listens to a beacon 0.1% range, 0.1–1° bearing <¥1k BOM (open source) Diver follow-me, AUV navigation LBL (seafloor) 3+ seafloor transponders, multilateration Sub-meter (range-independent) $50k+ Fixed-site survey DVL Doppler velocity log, dead reckoning Drifts over hours $5k+ Combined with USBL/LBL How piUSBL works # In the inverted (on-board) configuration, the robot carries a compact hydrophone array while the diver wears a small acoustic beacon that periodically emits short pulses. The robot measures the Time Difference of Arrival (TDOA) of each pulse across its hydrophones, solves the beacon’s relative bearing, and fuses the result with an on-board pressure sensor for depth. Because the robot only listens and never transmits, it consumes very little power and does not betray its position.
Two landmark papers established this approach:
Rypkema et al. (MIT/IROS 2019) validated piUSBL accuracy in controlled experiments: ~0.1% range accuracy (0.1 m error at 100 m), ~1° bearing accuracy, and hundreds of meters of operating range using a 5-hydrophone pyramidal array. The system is broadcast-based — one beacon can localize N robots simultaneously. Wang et al. (Zhejiang University, IEEE RA-L 2022) engineered a full piUSBL system on a disc-shaped AUV and sea-tested it in the South China Sea — the direct engineering predecessor of the open-source Raspi2USBL project. The open-source Raspi2USBL (2025) reimplements the same architecture on a Raspberry Pi with four hydrophones, achieving 1.3 km tracking for under ¥1000 in parts.
Reference case: iBubble. The commercial iBubble follow-me drone used exactly this architecture: a 4-hydrophone piUSBL + pressure sensor fusion, 1.5–6 m follow range (25 m max), 60 m depth rating, 90 min endurance, 9 kg mass, and a 90-second lost-signal auto-surface safety behavior.
Engineering applications # Jiaolong manned submersible — USBL + LBL combined navigation. Jiaolong, China’s first 7,000-meter-class manned submersible, uses a combined USBL + LBL scheme. A USBL transducer on the mother ship tracks the submersible in real time, while a seabed LBL transponder array provides high-precision calibration. Sea trials show LBL accuracy exceeds USBL, but USBL is far more flexible to deploy — the two complement each other.
Miniature USBL transducers for consumer ROVs. With MEMS and miniaturization, USBL transducers are now palm-sized. Advanced Navigation’s Subsonus, for example, is about 10 cm in diameter and under 1 kg, mounts directly on small ROVs or AUVs, delivers sub-meter positioning, and suits shallow near-shore operations.
Open source: Raspi2USBL. A Raspberry Pi-based open-source USBL positioning project designed for underwater robots. Sea trials report a maximum localization range of about 1300 m with stable slant range and bearing measurements. The project closely resembles a single-frequency (e.g. 70 kHz) transmit-receive scheme — low-cost hardware validating acoustic positioning.
Industrial solutions at a glance # System Vendors Accuracy Range Use case USBL Sonardyne, Kongsberg Sub-meter to meter Kilometers Ship-based tracking of ROV/AUV LBL Sonardyne, Oceaneering cm–dm Hundreds of meters Fixed-area high-precision operations Miniature USBL Advanced Navigation, EvoLogics Meter level Hundreds of meters Small ROV/AUV near-shore operations Open source Raspi2USBL, piUSBL Meter level Tens to hundreds of meters Research, prototype validation Product landscape # Platform Type Positioning Depth Price SoFi (MIT) Research prototype BFSK remote 18 m Research iBubble evo Follow-me drone piUSBL 60 m ~$2999 FIFISH V-EVO Tethered ROV AI vision lock 100 m $1399 FIFISH V6 Plus Tethered ROV Dual sonar + USBL 100 m ~$2000 Hydrus Autonomous ROV DVL + USBL + INS 300 m Professional Slocum glider Research platform Dead reckoning + GPS surfacing 1000 m Research Raspi2USBL Open source piUSBL Lab <¥1k BOM A notable trend: consumer follow-me platforms such as the FIFISH V-EVO have moved toward AI vision lock rather than pure acoustic follow, suggesting that acoustic-only follow has not yet become mainstream at the consumer price point.
Obstacle-avoidance sonar # Short-range obstacle detection (0.5–6 m) is mandatory on every untethered platform:

Why acoustic communication? # Underwater acoustic communication is the technology that uses sound waves to carry information through water. Electromagnetic waves (radio, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth) attenuate extremely fast in seawater — practical ranges are usually a few meters at most. Sound, by contrast, propagates hundreds of meters to tens of kilometers in the ocean, making it the only practical wireless medium underwater. The field has been developing for over a century, from early underwater bell navigation to modern underwater sensor networks.
The underwater acoustic channel # The underwater acoustic channel is one of the most challenging in communications:
Characteristic Description Consequence Slow propagation ~1500 m/s, 1/200,000 of the speed of light Large propagation delay, poor real-time performance Severe attenuation Higher frequencies attenuate faster Narrow usable bandwidth, usually a few kHz Multipath Reflections from surface and seabed Signal distortion, inter-symbol interference Doppler Relative motion shifts frequency Receiver must track frequency Ambient noise Waves, marine life, ship noise Low SNR, high bit-error rate System structure # A typical system consists of: transmitter (signal source → modulation → power amplifier → transducer), the acoustic channel, and receiver (transducer → preamplifier → demodulation → data processing). The core of the whole chain is modulation — how digital bits are encoded into sound.
The sonar equation # Every acoustic system — communication modems, pingers, positioning arrays — obeys the same energy balance:
$$SL - 2TL + TS - (NL - DI) = DT$$where $SL$ is the source level, $TL$ the transmission loss, $TS$ the target strength (receiver sensitivity for communication links), $NL$ the ambient noise, $DI$ the array directivity gain, and $DT$ the detection threshold. Two mechanisms drive the transmission loss: spreading loss (about 6 dB per doubling of distance) and absorption loss, which rises sharply with frequency:
Frequency Absorption Loss at 10 m 10 kHz ~3 dB/km negligible 30 kHz 10–20 dB/km 0.2 dB 100 kHz ~100 dB/km 1 dB 200 kHz ~300 dB/km 3 dB To increase range, you either raise the source level, improve processing (lower $DT$), or use a directional array (higher $DI$).
OOK (On-Off Keying) # Principle: the simplest scheme. Presence of a carrier means 1, absence means 0. Analogy: a flashlight — on is 1, off is 0.
Transmitter: for an input bitstream such as 10111001 — bit 1 turns on the carrier and emits a 75 kHz sine burst; bit 0 turns it off.
Receiver: samples the signal, estimates energy; above threshold → 1, below → 0.
Pros: simplest to implement, low hardware cost, low power. Cons: poor noise immunity, vulnerable to interference, low data rate. Use case: low-speed short-range links, simple remote control, ranging pulses. FSK (Frequency Shift Keying) # Principle: different carrier frequencies represent bits. Frequency f1 means 0, frequency f2 means 1. Analogy: a whistle — low note is 0, high note is 1.
Transmitter: bit 0 emits f1 (e.g. 70 kHz), bit 1 emits f2 (e.g. 75 kHz).
Receiver: samples the signal, passes it through two band-pass filters for f1 and f2; the stronger output decides the bit.
Pros: better noise immunity than OOK; no precise phase synchronization needed. Cons: wide bandwidth, frequency switching takes time, medium data rate. Use case: medium/low-speed links where interference resistance matters. PSK (Phase Shift Keying) # Principle: phase changes represent bits. In basic BPSK: phase 0° is 0, phase 180° is 1. Analogy: clapping — clap with the left hand for 0, right hand for 1; frequency and amplitude stay unchanged, only the starting direction flips.
Transmitter: bit 0 emits a normal-phase carrier; bit 1 emits an inverted (180°) carrier.
Receiver: needs a local reference carrier; multiplies it with the received signal — same phase gives a positive voltage (0), opposite phase gives a negative voltage (1).
Pros: high spectral efficiency (higher rate than OOK/FSK at the same bandwidth), strong noise immunity. Cons: complex to implement, needs precise carrier synchronization, sensitive to Doppler. Use case: medium/high-speed links, bandwidth-limited scenarios. OFDM (Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing) # Principle: splits a high-speed data stream into many low-speed streams, modulated onto a large set of mutually orthogonal subcarriers transmitted in parallel. Analogy: a wide road with dozens of lanes running cars simultaneously — each lane is slow, but the total throughput is high.
Characteristics:
Many subcarriers — typically dozens to hundreds. Each subcarrier may use BPSK/QPSK/QAM. Strong multipath resistance — each subcarrier’s low rate means little inter-symbol interference. High spectral efficiency — orthogonal subcarriers waste no bandwidth. Pros: highest data rate, strongest multipath resistance, the mainstream of modern underwater communication. Cons: most complex, needs DSP or FPGA processing, demanding synchronization. Use case: high-speed links, underwater sensor networks, real-time video. Comparison and selection # Scheme Controls Spectral efficiency Noise immunity Complexity Typical rate OOK Signal presence Low Weak Simplest Hundreds of bps FSK Signal frequency Medium-low Medium Simple Thousands of bps FH-FSK Frequency hopping across many carriers Medium Medium-high Medium 0.5–5 kbps PSK Signal phase Medium-high Strong Complex Tens of thousands of bps S2C chirp Linear frequency sweep, spread spectrum High Strong Medium 7–62 kbps OFDM Parallel subcarriers Highest Strongest Most complex Hundreds of thousands of bps Selection from simple to complex, by need:
Ranging / simple on-off control → OOK is enough. Low-speed data with moderate interference → FSK. Medium/high-speed, limited bandwidth → PSK. High-speed with DSP capability → OFDM. The physical limit. The range–bandwidth trade-off is fundamental: kilometer-range links deliver about kbit/s, while 100-meter links manage tens of kbit/s. Even 60 kbit/s only carries CIF-quality video over roughly 300 m. Wireless high-definition video is not physically achievable underwater — untethered platforms store data on board and offload at the surface.
Technology roadmap # Era Milestone Significance Late 19th c. Underwater bell navigation Earliest acoustic communication — a bell near a lighthouse 1914 Fessenden echo ranging First use of sound to detect icebergs; the beginning of underwater acoustics 1940s WWII active sonar Anti-submarine detection; sonar matured 1981 DPSK underwater communication Digital modulation enters the field 2000s OFDM acoustic modems High-speed underwater communication takes off 2010s Software-defined acoustic modems Flexible, reconfigurable, multi-band 2020s Underwater sensor networks Multi-node networking, the underwater Internet of Things Trend: from analog to digital, from non-coherent to coherent, from single-carrier to multi-carrier, from point-to-point to networked. Modern systems widely adopt OFDM + MIMO; rates have grown from tens of bps to tens of kbps and beyond.
Foundational papers # Akyildiz, Pompili & Melodia (2005) — Underwater acoustic sensor networks: research challenges. The foundational survey of underwater acoustic sensor networks: systematically reviews channel characteristics (attenuation, multipath, Doppler), proposes the network architecture, and identifies MAC, routing, and localization as key challenges. It established the framework of the whole research field. (DOI)
Stojanovic (2009) — Underwater acoustic communications: Design considerations on the physical layer. Analyzes how the channel constrains physical-layer design, compares OOK/FSK/PSK performance in underwater channels, and discusses equalization and synchronization. The classic reference for modem design.
Kilfoyle & Baggeroer (2000) — The evolution of underwater acoustic communication. A historical review from WWII sonar to digital modulation, tracing the analog→digital, non-coherent→coherent evolution. The standard reference for the field’s development. (DOI)
Stojanovic & Preisig (2009) — Underwater acoustic communication channels: Propagation models and statistical characterization. Establishes propagation models and statistical characterization — multipath structure, delay spread, Doppler spread — the standard channel model for simulation and design. (DOI)
WHOI piUSBL (2015) — Passive inverted ultra-short baseline (piUSBL) localization. A surface beacon transmits periodically; the underwater vehicle carries only a receiving array and never transmits, measuring range and angle. Low power and cost on the underwater side — the mainstream low-cost localization scheme, later validated by MIT’s SandShark AUV.
Raspi2USBL (2025) — An open-source Raspberry Pi-based passive inverted ultra-short baseline positioning system. A fully open-source piUSBL implementation — hardware, firmware, and host software — dropping commercial USBL costs to the hundreds of yuan level. (GitHub, arXiv)
Jensen et al. (2016) — Software-defined underwater acoustic modems: Historical review and the NILUS approach. Proposes software-defined modems using general-purpose hardware plus configurable software, supporting multiple bands and modulation schemes, moving the field from dedicated hardware to a reconfigurable platform.
Transducer fundamentals # The transducer is the hardware core of any acoustic system — it converts electrical signals into sound waves (transmission) and back (reception):
Hydrophone: receives sound pressure and converts it to voltage. Projector (transmit transducer): amplifies and radiates electrical signals as acoustic energy. Piezoelectric ceramic: the most common transducer material, exploiting the reversible piezoelectric effect. Directivity index: how focused the beam is. Narrow beams give high gain but require precise aiming; wide beams cover more area but are less sensitive. Operating frequency: determines both transducer size and range — high-frequency transducers are small but short-ranged. References # Akyildiz I F, Pompili D, Melodia T. summary: Why acoustic communication? # Underwater acoustic communication is the technology that uses sound waves to carry information through water. Electromagnetic waves (radio, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth) attenuate extremely fast in seawater — practical ranges are usually a few meters at most. Sound, by contrast, propagates hundreds of meters to tens of kilometers in the ocean, making it the only practical wireless medium underwater. The field has been developing for over a century, from early underwater bell navigation to modern underwater sensor networks.

What is sound? # Sound is a mechanical disturbance propagating through an elastic medium. When a source vibrates, it compresses and expands adjacent medium particles periodically, forming alternating regions of compression and rarefaction that travel outward as longitudinal waves. Sound requires a medium — there is no sound propagation in vacuum.
Sound speed # Sound speed is determined by the elasticity and density of the medium:
$$c = \sqrt{K/\rho}$$where $c$ is the sound speed (m/s), $K$ the bulk modulus (Pa), and $\rho$ the density (kg/m³).
Medium Temperature Speed (m/s) Ratio to air Air 20 °C 343 1.0× Water 20 °C 1482 4.3× Seawater 20 °C, 3.5% salinity 1520 4.4× Steel Room temp ~5000 14.6× A useful note: in gases, sound speed changes noticeably with temperature (about +0.6 m/s per 1 °C); in liquids and solids the variation is much smaller.
Frequency classification # Category Frequency Typical use Infrasound < 20 Hz Seismic monitoring, typhoon warning, elephant communication Audible 20 Hz – 20 kHz Speech, music Ultrasound > 20 kHz Medical imaging, underwater sonar, ultrasonic cleaning Hyper-sound > 100 MHz High-frequency acoustic microscopy, non-destructive testing Frequency, wavelength, and wavenumber # Frequency $f$ is the number of vibration cycles per second (Hz). Wavelength $\lambda$ is the distance between adjacent in-phase points, related by:
$$\lambda = c / f$$The wavenumber $k = 2\pi/\lambda$ describes the rate of spatial phase change.
Wavelength and diffraction # Diffraction ability depends on the relative size of the obstacle and the wavelength:
Obstacle size vs λ Acoustic behavior Everyday example Obstacle « λ Sound almost fully bends around Subwoofer audible in the next room Obstacle ≈ λ Partial diffraction, partial reflection Hearing part of the sound around a corner Obstacle » λ Sound is blocked High-pitched notes need an open door Analogy: low-frequency long-wavelength sound behaves like a fog lamp — light scatters in all directions; high-frequency short-wavelength sound behaves like a flashlight beam — directional but poor at bending around obstacles.
Sound pressure level and decibels # Sound propagation causes pressure perturbations $p$ (Pa). The human ear perceives a huge dynamic range (roughly 10⁻⁵ to 10² Pa), so acoustics uses the logarithmic sound pressure level (SPL):
$$SPL = 20 \cdot \log_{10}(p/p_{ref}) \text{ dB}$$where the reference pressure $p_{ref} = 20\ \mu$Pa (the threshold of hearing in air).
Common SPL references # Environment SPL (dB) Subjective feeling Quiet recording studio 20 Almost silent Quiet residence 40 Peaceful Normal conversation (1 m) 60 Comfortable Busy street 80 Noisy Chainsaw / motorcycle 100 Uncomfortable; long exposure damages hearing Front row at concert 110–120 Pain threshold; can damage hearing instantly Rocket launch pad 160+ Risk of physical damage The logarithmic nature of decibels # SPL change Pressure ratio Energy ratio Subjective feeling +3 dB 1.41× 2× Barely noticeable +10 dB 3.16× 10× Perceived as roughly twice as loud +20 dB 10× 100× Significantly louder +40 dB 100× 10000× Entirely different magnitude Acoustic impedance and interface transmission # Acoustic impedance is the product of density and sound speed:
$$Z = \rho \cdot c \text{ (Rayl)}$$It determines how much of a wave reflects versus transmits at a boundary between two media.
Medium Density (kg/m³) Speed (m/s) Impedance (Rayl) Ratio to air Air (20 °C) 1.21 343 415 1 Water (20 °C) 998 1482 1.48×10⁶ 3566 Human soft tissue ~1060 ~1540 ~1.63×10⁶ 3928 Steel 7850 5000 3.93×10⁷ 94700 Impedance matching and transmission coefficient # At the interface between two media, the sound intensity transmission coefficient is approximately:
$$T = 4Z_1Z_2 / (Z_1 + Z_2)^2$$When $Z_1 \approx Z_2$, $T \approx 1$ and nearly all energy passes through. When the impedances differ greatly, $T \approx 0$ and nearly everything reflects.
Why medical ultrasound uses coupling gel # Air and human soft tissue differ in impedance by roughly 4000×. If an air layer sits between the probe and skin, transmission drops below 0.1%. The coupling gel applied before an ultrasound exam exists precisely to eliminate the air layer and match impedance.
Wave propagation behaviors # Reflection — at a sudden impedance change, part of the energy returns to the original medium. Hard surfaces (walls, rock, water surface) reflect strongly; soft absorbing materials (foam, fiber, carpet) reflect weakly. Echo is the perceivable reflected sound. Refraction — a wave changes direction when its speed changes across a medium interface, like light entering water. In the ocean, sound speed varies with depth, temperature, and salinity, forming a sound-speed profile that can trap waves in a deep channel (the SOFAR channel). Diffraction — sound bends around obstacle edges. Low-frequency long wavelengths diffract strongly, which is why infrasound can travel thousands of kilometers. Interference — two coherent waves superpose: in-phase positions reinforce, anti-phase positions cancel. Active noise cancellation (ANC) uses exactly this: a speaker emits a wave of equal amplitude and opposite phase to cancel the noise. Attenuation # Sound intensity weakens during propagation through two mechanisms:
Spherical spreading loss # A point source radiates a spherical wavefront. As distance $r$ grows, energy spreads over $4\pi r^2$, so intensity falls as $1/r^2$. In dB terms:
$$\Delta SPL = 20 \cdot \log_{10}(r_2/r_1) \text{ dB}$$Every doubling of distance costs about 6 dB (in free field).
Medium absorption # Viscosity and thermal conduction convert acoustic energy into heat; the absorption coefficient rises with frequency.
Frequency Air absorption (dB/100 m) Typical range 1 kHz ~1 Several km 10 kHz ~10 Hundreds of m 100 kHz ~100 Tens of m 1 MHz ~1000 A few m This is why underwater sonar operates in the tens-to-hundreds of kHz band: it balances propagation range against angular resolution.
Typical applications # Domain Core principle Key parameters Medical B-mode ultrasound Ultrasound reflection + impedance matching 3.5–15 MHz Underwater sonar / ranging Ultrasound reflection and propagation 20–200 kHz Active noise-cancelling headphones Wave interference cancellation 20–1000 Hz Ultrasonic cleaning / lithotripsy High-frequency cavitation 20–50 kHz Architectural acoustics Reflection and absorption control Reverberation time 0.5–2 s Infrasound early warning Long-wavelength infrasound propagation < 20 Hz References # 杜功焕, 朱哲民, 龚秀芬. 声学基础 (第三版). 南京大学出版社, 2001. 张海澜. 理论声学. 高等教育出版社, 2007. Why hull form matters # Figure 1. HUGIN Superior, a 6.6 m torpedo-shaped AUV with L/D ≈ 7.5. Note the smooth revolve body, hemispherical nose, tapered stern, and flush-mounted sensor windows. Image: Kongsberg.
An underwater vehicle’s resistance has three components:
Skin friction drag — proportional to wetted surface area and boundary layer state. Form drag / pressure drag — depends on whether the shape avoids flow separation. Wave-making drag — only significant near the surface. For an AUV cruising at 2–5 kn, form drag and friction drag are comparable. For an ROV moving below 2 kn with lots of appendages, the absolute drag is small, but the thruster power budget is tight enough that every streamlining decision still matters.
A streamlined hull directly affects three performance numbers:
Endurance — lower drag means more range per battery. MBARI Tethys reshaped its tail to delay separation and stretched AUV endurance from days to weeks; Slocum Sentinel Redwing plans 15,000 km single-segment crossings in 2025. Speed — VideoRay Pro 5, with a compact torpedo hull and rear main thruster, reaches >4.4 kn in its class, far above multi-vectored-rotor ROVs (~2 kn). Noise — a smooth hull with controlled separation lowers self-noise, which matters for survey AUVs carrying multibeam sonar and magnetometers. Kongsberg HUGIN Superior explicitly markets itself as a “very stable, low-noise hydrodynamic platform.” Engineering metrics of a “streamlined” hull # Metric Definition Typical values Slenderness L/D Overall length / max diameter Biological optimum 4–6; commercial AUV 8–12; multi-rotor ROV not applicable Profile shape Axial longitudinal section Myring body, NACA 66-67 laminar profile, ellipsoid Max diameter location Max diameter aft of nose / total length Biology 35–45%; engineered AUV ~40–50% Parallel mid-body fraction Parallel mid-section length / total length ≤30%, otherwise form drag rises sharply Appendages / openings Number of protrusions, sensor fairings Flush-mount, filleted edges is standard Surface treatment Fairing smoothness, riblets, compliant coating Smooth fairing baseline; riblets optional (+7–10% drag reduction) Strouhal number St = f · A / U (tailbeat · amplitude / speed) 0.2–0.4 for all efficient swimmers Five design routes # The 2015–2025 product landscape splits into five distinct philosophies:
Category Typical shape L/D Speed Design priority True streamlined AUV Torpedo revolve body (Bluefin, REMUS, HUGIN) 7–13 3–5 kn Low drag, low noise, long endurance Underwater glider Slender cylinder + wings (Slocum, Seaglider) 6–8 0.3–1 kn Ultra-low power, month-long missions Streamlined ROV (consumer) Ellipsoid / rounded box + multi-thruster (FIFISH, Chasing) L/W 1.1–2.0 1.5–4 kn 6-DOF hover, tool carrying Industrial transitional ROV Compact torpedo short hull (VideoRay) or cylinder + frame (Boxfish) — >4 kn High-speed inspection, modular payload Bio-inspired soft robot Tuna / dolphin / manta / boxfish shape (MIT, Festo, SJTU, ZJU) Biological 3–6 0.5–5 kn High maneuverability, low disturbance, biological efficiency The two most visually different philosophies sit at opposite ends of this table. A torpedo-shaped AUV (Bluefin-12S below left) is a smooth revolve body with no protrusions at all. An open-frame ROV (BlueROV2 below right) is an aluminum frame with every thruster, sensor, and battery exposed.
Figure 2 (top). Bluefin-12S: a 3.66 m yellow torpedo revolve body, L/D ≈ 11.3, designed for modular mine-countermeasure and ocean survey. Image: General Dynamics.
Figure 3 (bottom). BlueROV2 in the field: an open aluminum frame with six vectored thrusters, two plastic pressure housings, and an exposed camera. This is the reference open-frame platform used by universities and makers worldwide. Image: Blue Robotics.
Profile selection # The profile choice follows mission:
Long-endurance torpedo AUV / glider: Myring body (analytic fore-and-aft curves) or NACA 66/67 laminar profile revolve. Max diameter at 35–45% of length, parallel mid-body ≤30%. Bio-inspired BCF robot fish: NACA 63-015A / 67-021 profile-like body, max thickness at ~20% length, tail “necking” into caudal fin with reinforcing keels. Bio-inspired MPF robot (manta, penguin): Low-camber wing-like pectoral fins; body flattened or rounded. Key is lift efficiency of the fins, not the body. Boxfish-style payload hull: Do not force water streamlining; use fins / vectored thrusters to actively compensate for inherent instability. Slenderness ratio: biology vs engineering # Optimal low-drag range: L/D ≈ 4–6. Penguins 3–4, tuna 4–5.6, dolphins 4–5. Literature puts L/D = 5 as the point of minimum drag with parallel section ≤30%. Commercial AUV range: L/D ≈ 8–12 (longer than biology because payload and batteries demand internal volume). Bluefin-12S reaches 11.3, REMUS 600 10–13, HUGIN Endurance 10.9. Multi-rotor ROVs: L/D is not constrained; L/W ≈ 1.1–2.0 suffices because hover and tool carrying dominate. Engineering L/D trades biological optimum (4–6) for internal volume. This is the “battery and payload constraint” overriding the hydrodynamic optimum.
Surface treatment # Method Drag reduction Maturity Recommendation Smooth fairing + flush-mount sensors + filleted openings Baseline, removes protrusion drag Must-do All sensor ports, bolts, hatches flush Shark-skin riblet film 7–10% Available off-the-shelf Apply along flow direction, tune spacing to Re Dolphin compliant coating Delays transition to Re ~2×10⁷ Not mature (compliance matching unresolved) Watch literature Tuna mucus / smooth lubricant coating ~15% cruise-speed gain in biology Process simple, gain small Optional, not critical path Tail and propulsion matching # Tail type Use case Efficiency High-aspect-ratio lunate tail (tuna, marlin, mako) High-speed cruise Lift-based thrust, low induced drag Fork / square tail (barracuda, boxfish) High maneuver, acceleration Drag-based, agile but inefficient MPF pectoral oscillation (manta) Low-speed long-endurance gliding High lift efficiency, can turn in place Undulating long-based fin (cutlassfish, BionicFinWave) Pipeline / fine intervention Low disturbance, full maneuverability Single propeller on revolve body (AUV standard) Medium-high speed cruise Axisymmetric, requires stern taper All efficient biological swimmers share a Strouhal window St = 0.2–0.4. The mechanical design should land in this band.
Appendage penalty: three-layer compensation # Consumer ROVs represent a compromise: a rounded ellipsoid shell that streamlines the body but leaves six vectored thrusters protruding. FIFISH V6 below is the canonical example — a fluorescent-yellow boll-shell with corner thrusters, designed for 6-DOF hover rather than minimum drag.
Figure 4. FIFISH V6 (QYSEA): a 383×331×143 mm boll-shell ROV with four corner and two side vectored thrusters. The rounded shell reduces drag compared with a square frame, but the thruster barrels remain protrusions. Image: QYSEA / Underwater Australasia.
Payload openings, sensor windows, and thruster barrels inevitably break the clean hull. Engineering compensates in three layers:
Flush-mount — every sensor window, bolt, and hatch sits coplanar with the shell. Gliders even put GPS/Iridium antennas inside the wing to eliminate external dome drag. Fillet all openings — avoid sharp corners that trigger separation. Drag budget decomposition — use towing tank / CFD to identify each drag source and fix them one by one. REMUS is the textbook case: successive towing-tank tests identified sources, and sealed-propeller thrusters were the final improvement. What the last decade changed # Four methodological generations:
Era Years Methods Mark Empirical revolve body Pre-2015 Myring (1976) / Hoerner formulas, hand-picked NACA profiles L/D 5–7 by rule of thumb CFD era 2015–2018 RANS (k–ε / k–ω SST), 2D/3D unstructured mesh, towing-tank validation Parametric profiles, still hand-tuned Optimization era 2019–2022 Bezier / Myring parametrization + GA / Bayesian / NSGA-II + surrogate model; GAN-generated hulls from 2022 Multi-objective (drag + volume + stability) auto-searched Digital twin 2023–2025 CFD (LES/DNS explaining transition), pool + sea trials, DRL trained in simulation then deployed Sim-to-real closed loop, morphology self-adapts Hardware trends:
3D printing (FDM/SLS): PLA/PA12 outer skins shrink complex hull iterations from months to days. Harbin Engineering University printed an 85 cm AUV hull for under ¥10,000. Composite monocoque: Gliders (e.g. SeaWing 7000 m) use carbon/epoxy shells that hold 6000 m pressure while staying hydrodynamically smooth. Bio-inspired soft bodies: Tunabot Flex (2021) showed body flexibility cuts cost of transport 53% over rigid multi-joint fish; Festo BionicFinWave (2020) commercialized undulating fin propulsion. Reference products by mission # Long endurance / high speed: Bluefin-9 (L/D 6.9), REMUS 100 (L/D 8.4), MBARI Tethys (L/D 7.7, week-long missions). Near-bottom / high maneuver: VideoRay Pro 5 (>4.4 kn), Deep Trekker Revolution (rounded ellipsoid carbon hull), Boxfish Luna (1000 m cinematic ROV). Bio-inspired agile: Tunabot Flex, Festo Airacuda, SJTU robotic dolphin, HEU eel-like soft robot. Further reading # Myring body equations — the analytic revolve-body parametric form. Bluefin Robotics / General Dynamics AUVs — product line. Kongsberg HUGIN AUV series — commercial deep-water standard. Slocum Glider, Teledyne Webb — long-endurance platform. Tunabot Flex, Science Robotics 2021 — soft-body fish efficiency study. Festo BionicFinWave — undulating fin ROV. Blue Robotics BlueROV2 — the open-frame reference platform.

What is FreeRTOS? # FreeRTOS is a free, open-source real-time operating system kernel designed for microcontrollers and small microprocessors. It manages multiple tasks on a single CPU, deciding which task runs, when it runs, and for how long. The core is small — typically a few hundred lines of C plus architecture-specific assembly — and it runs directly on the hardware without an MMU.
Official documentation: freertos.org. Source code: github.com/FreeRTOS/FreeRTOS-Kernel.
Why an RTOS? # On a bare-metal loop, the application calls functions sequentially in main(). Adding sensors, networking, and user input means either a giant switch-case state machine or cooperative multitasking where every function must yield. Both become fragile as the system grows: a slow I2C read blocks everything else.
An RTOS lets the developer write independent tasks that run concurrently. The kernel handles timing, priorities, and blocking. A control loop can run at a fixed 1 kHz rate while a log task handles UART output at its own pace, without the programmer writing explicit timing glue.
Task scheduling: preemptive priority # FreeRTOS uses preemptive priority-based scheduling:
The scheduler always runs the highest-priority ready task. If a lower-priority task is running and a higher-priority task becomes ready, the kernel immediately context-switches to the higher task. Tasks of equal priority take turns in time slices (round-robin), if configUSE_TIME_SLICING is enabled. This means the developer assigns priorities based on how time-critical each task is. A motor control loop gets the highest priority; a display refresh gets the lowest.
A direct consequence: a high-priority task that never blocks will starve every lower-priority task. Every time-critical task must call a blocking API — vTaskDelay(), xSemaphoreTake(), ulTaskNotifyTake(), or a queue receive — to release the CPU when it has nothing to do.
Task states # At any moment, a task is in one of four states:
State Meaning Running Currently executing on the CPU. Only one task runs at a time. Ready Runnable, waiting for CPU time because a higher-priority task holds it. Blocked Waiting for an event — a delay to expire, a semaphore, a queue message, or a notification. Suspended Explicitly suspended via vTaskSuspend(). Does not participate in scheduling until resumed. A task in Blocked or Suspended state consumes zero CPU. This is how an RTOS achieves low power: idle tasks enter sleep, and the kernel wakes them only when an event arrives.
Context switching # Each task has its own stack. When the scheduler swaps tasks:
The current task’s CPU registers (program counter, stack pointer, general-purpose registers) are pushed onto that task’s stack. The stack pointer is switched to the next task’s stack. The saved registers are popped from the new task’s stack. Execution resumes exactly where that task left off. This happens entirely in hardware-assisted assembly (PendSV on ARM Cortex-M). The application code sees a continuous call stack and does not know a switch occurred. Context switch cost is typically a few microseconds on a 100 MHz Cortex-M4.
A practical task layout # A typical motor-control or robot firmware might look like:
Task Priority Responsibility ControlTask Highest (e.g. 5) Reads IMU, runs PID / RL policy, writes motor commands at 1 kHz. CommTask Medium (3) Receives commands over UART/CAN, sends telemetry. LogTask Low (1) Formats and writes logs to SD card or USB. Idle 0 (auto) Kernel-created; can run low-power hooks or clean up. The control task blocks on a hardware timer semaphore each cycle. The communication task blocks on a UART queue. The log task blocks on a log queue. When nothing needs attention, the idle task runs and the microcontroller can enter sleep.
Inter-task communication # Tasks rarely work in isolation. FreeRTOS provides several primitives:
Queues — thread-safe FIFO buffers. One task writes, another reads. Data is copied, not passed by reference, which avoids race conditions. Semaphores — binary or counting. Used to signal an event from an ISR to a task, or to limit access to a shared resource. Mutexes — like a binary semaphore but with priority inheritance. If a low-priority task holds a mutex that a high-priority task wants, the low task temporarily gets the high priority until it releases the mutex. This reduces priority inversion. Task notifications — a lightweight, per-task signal that avoids allocating a queue. Faster and uses less RAM than a queue when only one event source exists. Event groups — set or clear bits; a task can wait for multiple conditions simultaneously. Memory management # The kernel itself needs RAM for task stacks, TCBs (task control blocks), queues, and semaphores. FreeRTOS ships with several heap implementations:
heap_1 — allocate only, never free. Simplest, used when tasks are created once and never deleted. heap_2 — allocate and free, but does not coalesce adjacent free blocks. Deprecated. heap_4 — allocate and free with coalescing. The most common choice for dynamic systems. heap_5 — like heap_4 but can span multiple non-contiguous memory regions. For safety-critical or predictable systems, tasks can also be created statically: all memory is declared at compile time, and the kernel never calls malloc.
Interrupts and the kernel # ISRs must be short. They cannot call most blocking APIs directly. FreeRTOS provides FromISR variants (e.g. xQueueSendFromISR()) that are safe to call from interrupt context. At the end of an ISR, a portYIELD_FROM_ISR() macro triggers a context switch if a higher-priority task was woken by the ISR.
Further reading # FreeRTOS Official Website — API reference and kernel docs. FreeRTOS User Guide (PDF) — official manual. FreeRTOS-Kernel on GitHub — source code and porting layers. Mastering the FreeRTOS Real Time Kernel — the standard textbook, freely available from the kernel maintainer.

Project Overview # In nature, fish employ high-acceleration, explosive fast-start maneuvers—typically executing a primary body bend within several milliseconds and an expansive release within tens of milliseconds—to escape predators or strike prey. However, conventional control paradigms struggle to reproduce these high-burst, non-periodic, and omnidirectional agile trajectories due to the rigid phase constraints of synchronized gaits.
To address this challenge, this study introduces BASS (Bio-inspired Agile Start-up Strategy), a novel omnidirectional fast-start control framework governed by deep reinforcement learning. By directly mapping joint actuation within a data-driven action space, the framework harnesses highly nonlinear fluid-structure interaction forces. This method enables the robot to execute explosive transient turns and forward bursts across a comprehensive range of target headings, effectively bridging the Sim2Real transfer gap inherent in unsteady, transient hydrodynamic environments.
Algorithm & Architecture Design: The framework entirely bypasses traditional gait generators, such as Central Pattern Generators (CPGs), by mapping the action space directly to the target positions of the driving joints. This unconstrained, non-periodic formulation grants the policy maximum autonomy to explore and synthesize highly dynamic, agile gaits within non-linear fluid domains.
Bio-inspired Reward Mechanism: Integrated with a high-fidelity CFD fluid solver, the complex physical process of a fast-start is explicitly partitioned into two distinct biological phases to guide multi-objective reward formulation. Stage I (the bending phase) concentrates on angular velocity adjustments to rapidly minimize heading errors for optimal turning, while Stage II (the stretching phase) focuses on linear velocity along the target vector to unlock stored potential energy for explosive acceleration.
Policy Deployment & Generalization: The framework establishes a high-dimensional state space incorporating robot kinematics, real-time joint feedback, and phase markers. By incorporating domain randomization schedules across initial poses, orientations, and target headings during training, the network effectively accommodates modeling discrepancies in transient fluid-structure interactions, ultimately enabling zero-shot policy migration to physical aquatic environments.
Technical Stack
Algorithm Framework : Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) / BASS Policy / Markov Decision Process (MDP) / PyTorch
Fluid Simulation : CFD Fluid Solver / Unsteady Hydrodynamics / Fluid-Structure Interaction (FSI) / Vortex Visualization
Policy Transfer : Bio-inspired Reward Design / Domain Randomization / Sim2Real Migration
Video Demonstration # These videos demonstrate the comprehensive academic findings of this study alongside physical deployment clips validating explosive fast-start capabilities on a multi-joint robotic fish platform.

Core Capabilities # Non-Periodic Omnidirectional Burst Control: By specifying the action space directly as the desired target positions of each articulating joint, the algorithm liberates itself from the rigid cyclical constraints of standard locomotion. This configuration yields a highly flexible policy capable of discovering non-periodic, transient maneuvers, granting the robot exceptional agility across broad target heading angles.
Bio-inspired Two-Stage Optimization: The network leverages a coupled, phase-specific multi-objective reward structure. During the initial bending phase (Stage I), the policy prioritizes angular velocity responses to minimize heading deviations, optimizing C-shape body deformations. In the subsequent stretching phase (Stage II), the objective shifts to maximizing linear velocity along the target path, channeling fluid momentum into explosive forward propulsion.
High-Fidelity Sim2Real Migration: High-dimensional physical state vectors—capturing robot kinematics, joint feedback, and transient phase indicators—serve as the foundation for the reinforcement learning observation space. Evaluated at a fixed closed-loop control frequency, the framework leverages advanced domain randomization to mitigate fluid-structure modeling errors induced by complex, unsteady wake vortices and mechanical backlashes, achieving robust zero-shot physical deployment.
Optimized Fluidic Wake Structure: High-fidelity CFD visualizations confirm that under the BASS framework, the robotic platform generates a prominent, non-linear attached vortex during the initial body-bend phase. Upon extension, these structures cleanly shed to form a structured reverse Kármán vortex street, yielding instantaneous energy transfer efficiencies and axial displacements that significantly outperform baseline periodic gaits with fixed phase differences.
Conclusion & Future Work # Feasibility of Non-Periodic Agile Maneuvers: This work successfully demonstrates that deep reinforcement learning (DRL) architectures can autonomously synthesize transient, non-periodic escape responses and adaptive fast-start profiles for multi-joint robotic fish operating in unsteady fluid environments. Efficacy of Bio-inspired Reward Formulations: Experimental results confirm that embedding biological two-stage (bend-and-stretch) mechanics into the Markov Decision Process (MDP) reward topology produces superior directional targeting accuracy and greater forward propulsion displacement compared to structured gait baselines. Future Research Directions: Enhancing policy robustness and online adaptation under severe fluidic disturbances, including unstructured environmental currents, unsteady turbulence, and wild field conditions. Investigating the co-design of advanced flexible structural mechanics, compliant smart materials, and rigid multi-joint architectures to further expand peak mechanical energy transfer during transient agile maneuvers.

Project Introduction # Inspired by the streamlined body and efficient swimming patterns of the barracuda, I designed and developed the Brizo bionic robotic fish platform. I independently managed the entire development cycle, from conceptual sketching to a fully functional prototype. Measuring 0.5 meters in length, this platform integrates mechanical structures, embedded hardware, and advanced motion control algorithms, providing a comprehensive experimental platform for validating bionic propulsion and autonomous movement.
Mechanical & Modeling: Designed the multi-joint bionic structure and streamlined hull using SolidWorks; constructed URDF models for simulation alignment. Utilized static sealing technology to achieve IP68 waterproofing, ensuring stable operation of internal systems under dynamic loads for ≥1 hour.
Embedded & Hardware Development: Built around the ESP32-S3, I completed the schematic and PCB designs, including power distribution and actuator control circuits. Powered by an 8.4V LiPo battery with DC-DC regulation. Implemented a CAN (TWAI) network for unified servo control and integrated an IMU for real-time attitude feedback. Designed a dual-link system with 915MHz (CRSF) for long-range control and WiFi (AsyncUDP) for real-time debugging, achieving stable 50Hz motion control.
Motion Control Algorithms: Developed a multi-joint coordinated propulsion algorithm based on Central Pattern Generators (CPG), optimizing efficiency through parameter identification to reach a cruise speed of 0.5 m/s. Conducted Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) training within a CFD (Computational Fluid Dynamics) simulator and validated Sim2Real transfer methods for deploying simulation-trained policies onto the physical robot.
Technical Stack
Mechanical : SolidWorks / URDF / IP68 Waterproofing / 3D Printing
Hardware : ESP32-S3 / PCB Design (LCEDA) / CAN (TWAI)
Algorithms : CPG Algorithm / CFD Fluid Simulation / Deep Reinforcement Learning / Sim2Real

Reaches a cruise speed of 0.5 m/s, offering superior maneuverability and stealth compared to traditional propellers. Dual-Link Communication: Parallel 915MHz long-range control and WiFi debugging links support both outdoor deployment and real-time indoor parameter tuning.
